newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan establishes diplomatic ties with Sao Tome.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan establishes diplomatic ties with Sao Tome.

text.p: Taiwan on Tuesday said it had established formal ties with West Africa's small twin-island nation of Sao Tome and Principe, scoring a minor victory in its four-decade diplomatic tug-of-war with arch rival China.
"The Republic of China has established full diplomatic relations with Sao Tome and Principe," Foreign Minister John Chang told a news conference in Taipei.

The announcement brings to 31 the number of countries that maintain official relations with Taiwan's exiled Republic of China, although that number will fall back to 30 later this year when South Africa switches ties to communist China.
The move was sure to anger China which has viewed Taiwan as a rebel-held province after a civil war split them in 1949, and has warned other countries against forging ties with Taipei.
The African nation had maintained diplomatic ties with Beijing before switching recognition to Taipei.

Chang and his Sao Tome counterpart M. Homero Salvaterra, who arrived in Taipei on Sunday, signed and exchanged copies of a recognition joint communique during a ceremony at Taiwan's foreign ministry on Tuesday.
"For years, (Sao Tome) has desired to establish formal ties with us," the ministry said in a statement.
"The sides will have full economic, technology, medical and agriculture cooperation in the future, which will enable the two countries to increase their ties," the ministry said.
It said Sao Tome and Taiwan decided to establish official ties "based on equal and reciprocal principles and a common wish of developing friendly relations."
The ministry also said the political climate in Sao Tome was stable and democracy established. It added that the African nation had good potential for economic development.
Sao Tome and Principe, a former Portuguese colony 200 km (125 miles) off the coast of Gabon, is one of the poorest countries in the world and heavily depends on foreign aid.
It became independent from Portugal in 1975, and in 1991 held its first presidential and multi-partisan congress elections.
The African country has a foreign debt of US$340 million, which it is unable to finance, and desperately needs aid to fund development projects.

Nationalist Taiwan and China have competed aggressively, especially in Africa, for diplomatic recognition since 1949, often accusing each other of using large sums of cash and aid to woo potential backers.
In the past five years, another poor Afrian nation, Niger, switched ties twice -- first to Taipei from Beijing in 1992 and then back to Beijing in 1996.
